title: Free Performance Review Templates & Forms
summary: Free performance review templates for manager, self, peer and quarterly reviews. Copy the blank form, see a filled example, and download it in Word or PDF.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


- A performance review template is a reusable form that sets the same questions, competencies and rating scale for everyone in a cycle. Copy the full form off this page or download it in Word or PDF.
- Ten sections: employee details, rating scale, goals and results, competencies with an evidence field, strengths, areas to improve, development goals, reviewer summary, employee comments and sign-off.
- Four variants included: manager, self-review, peer and quarterly. Each changes the prompts, not the structure.
- A filled example shows what an evidence-backed answer and rating look like in every field.
- Rating scale options compared: 3-point, 5-point, 4-point and behaviorally anchored, with the failure mode of each.
- Templates standardize the form. They do not automate distribution, reminders, collection or reporting, which is what performance review software does.


A performance review template is a reusable form that sets the same questions, competencies and rating scale for every employee in a cycle. Whether your organization calls it a performance review form, an employee evaluation form or an appraisal form, it is the same artifact. This page gives you that form three ways: a full version you can copy straight off the page, an editable Word file, and a printable PDF. Below the template you will find a filled example, four variants for manager, self, peer and quarterly reviews, rating scale options, and a checklist for adapting the form to your own roles.


Free download


## Get the performance review template


One employee performance review form covering details, goals, competencies, ratings, strengths, development plan and sign-off. Editable and free to reuse.


Takes one short form. The full template is also written out on this page if you would rather copy and paste it.


## Performance review form fields: what is included


Before the fields, a word on naming, because it causes more confusion than it should. Performance review form, performance evaluation form, employee appraisal form, employee review form and performance assessment form all describe the same document. Some organizations reserve “appraisal” for the annual pay-linked review and “review” for the wider conversation, but the fields underneath do not change. Use whichever term your organization already uses, and use one of them consistently.


The form has ten sections. Each one exists because a review that skips it tends to produce a rating nobody can explain later. Use the table to decide what to keep before you hand the form to managers.


Section What it captures Why it is in the form


Employee and review details Name, role, department, reviewer, review period, review type Makes the record searchable later and fixes the window being assessed


Rating scale The labels and definitions used everywhere else in the form Two managers reading “meets expectations” differently is the most common source of unfair ratings


Goals and results Each goal, its target, what was delivered, a rating Separates outcomes from effort, and stops the review becoming a personality assessment


Competencies and behaviors How the work was done, with an evidence field beside every rating The evidence column is what makes a rating defensible in a calibration meeting


Strengths Two or three strengths with situation, action and result Specific praise is repeatable. “Great attitude” is not


Areas to improve One or two behaviors and what better would look like Keeping it short forces the reviewer to pick what actually matters


Development goals Goal, support needed, success measure, target date Turns the review into an input for the next cycle rather than a verdict on the last one


Reviewer summary and overall rating A short narrative plus the overall rating and any recommended action Gives HR and calibration a single consistent field to read across the population


Employee comments The employee’s own response, written after the conversation Documents disagreement at the time rather than months later


Acknowledgement Signatures and dates Confirms the review was discussed, which is not the same as agreeing with it


## Filled performance review example


Here is the same form completed for a fictional employee, Priya Nair, a mid-level account manager on a twelve-month cycle. The notes in purple explain why each answer works. Nothing here is real customer data.


Field Completed answer Why it works


Goal 1: renewal rate Target 88 percent. Delivered 91 percent across a book of 34 accounts, including two at-risk renewals recovered in Q3. Rating 4. The number, the scope and the hardest case are all named, so the rating does not rest on the reviewer’s memory


Goal 2: expansion revenue Target 120,000. Delivered 84,000. Two of the three expansion plays stalled when the buying committee changed. Rating 2. A missed goal is stated plainly with the cause, which is what makes the next conversation useful instead of defensive


Competency: collaboration Rebuilt the handover checklist with the onboarding team after three accounts launched late. Late launches went from three in Q1 to zero in Q3 and Q4. Rating 5. Evidence, a before figure and an after figure. This is what a rating of 5 has to look like to survive calibration


Competency: communication Account notes are consistently thorough. Escalations to the manager often arrive after the customer has already raised the issue rather than before. Rating 3. Balanced. Names one strength and one specific gap in the same field, instead of a vague “could communicate more”


Strength When the payments integration broke in October, Priya wrote the customer-facing update within two hours and the account renewed the following month. Situation, action, result. Short enough to be repeated back to the employee word for word


Area to improve Risk is flagged late. For the next two quarters, log every at-risk account in the pipeline review the week the signal appears, not the week before renewal. Describes a behavior and states the change in a way that can be observed, so progress can be checked at the next review


Development goal Run discovery on three enterprise accounts by June 30. Support needed: two joint calls with the enterprise lead. Measure: one qualified enterprise opportunity created. Support and a success measure are both named, which is what separates a development goal from a wish


Overall rating and summary Rating 3. Strong retention year with expansion below target. The retention work is genuinely above the level of the role. The next cycle should hold retention steady while rebuilding the expansion pipeline earlier. The summary explains the number rather than repeating it, and points at the next period


## Manager performance review template


The manager version is the generic form with the evidence burden moved onto the reviewer. The manager owns the final rating, so every rating field needs a written example beside it. Add these four prompts to the base template.


- **Results against agreed goals.** What was the target, what landed, and what changed during the period that either helped or got in the way?
- **How the results were achieved.** One example per competency. If you cannot write an example, the rating is a guess.
- **Comparison to level.** Is this performance at, below or above what the role level expects? Say which, and against which expectation.
- **Decision and next step.** Promotion, raise, development plan, or none. State it in the form rather than leaving it to a separate conversation.


If you are writing the summary and want wording to work from, the[performance review examples](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/performance-review-examples/) library has phrases sorted by competency and rating level. For the meeting itself, the[performance review preparation guide](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/prepare-for-performance-review/) covers what to bring and how to open.


## Self-review template


A self-review is not a shorter manager review. It asks for information the manager does not have: what the employee attempted, what they learned, and what they need. Keep it to five prompts so people actually complete it.


Prompt What you are asking for


What are you most proud of this period, and why? The work the employee thinks mattered, which is often not the work on the goal sheet


Which goal was hardest, and what happened? Context on a miss, in the employee’s words, before the manager writes a rating


What did you learn or get better at? Growth that has not shown up in results yet


What do you want to work on next, and why that? The starting point for the development section


What support would make the biggest difference? A specific, actionable ask directed at the manager or the organization


Employees filling this in for the first time usually need wording help more than they need more prompts. Point them at the[employee self assessment examples](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/self-evaluation-examples/) library rather than expanding the form.


## Peer review template


Peer feedback goes wrong when it asks colleagues to rate performance they cannot see. Restrict the peer form to observed working behavior and drop the overall rating entirely.


- How did you work with this person during the period? One or two sentences of context.
- Describe one occasion when working with them made your work easier or better.
- What is one thing they could do differently that would help the people around them?
- Rate collaboration, communication and reliability only, on the same scale as the main form.
- Optional: anything the manager should know that would not come up otherwise.


Peer input is one of several review formats. If you are still deciding which formats to run, the guide to[types of performance reviews](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/types-of-performance-reviews/) compares them side by side.


## Quarterly performance review template


A quarterly review should take fifteen minutes to fill in. Cut the competency grid, keep the goals, and add one forward-looking field. Ratings are optional at this cadence and many teams are better off without them.


- **Goals this quarter:** on track, at risk, or done. One line each.
- **What went well:** one specific thing.
- **What got in the way:** one specific thing, and whether it is still there.
- **Focus for next quarter:** no more than three priorities.
- **Support needed:** one ask.


If you are setting the calendar rather than the form, the[performance review cycle guide](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/performance-review-cycle-guide/) covers how quarterly check-ins and the annual review fit together.


### Want all four variants in one file?


The download includes the base template. Swap the competency grid for the prompts above to build the manager, self, peer or quarterly version in about two minutes.


## Performance review rating scale options


The scale matters more than the rest of the form. Most disagreement in calibration comes from two managers using the same label to mean different things. Pick one scale, define each point in writing on the review form itself, and use it everywhere.


Scale Points Use it when Watch out for


3-point Below, meets, exceeds Small teams, or a first cycle where you want managers to commit to a direction rather than a number Almost everyone lands on “meets”, so the scale stops distinguishing anything


5-point 1 not meeting, 2 partially meeting, 3 meeting, 4 exceeding, 5 outstanding The default for most organizations. Enough range for calibration and for compensation decisions Central tendency. Managers cluster on 3 unless you require evidence for every rating


4-point No midpoint: below, approaching, meets, exceeds You want to force a call one way or the other Removing the middle can push borderline performers up rather than down


Behaviorally anchored Each point carries a written description of the behavior at that level, per competency Competencies that managers interpret very differently, or roles with a formal leveling framework Slow to write and slow to maintain. Build it for four or five competencies, not twenty


Whichever you choose, write the definition into the form itself rather than into a separate policy document. A scale defined at the top of the page is a scale managers actually read. The template above ships with the 5-point version already filled in.


## How to customize a performance review template


A generic template is a starting point, not a policy. Work through this checklist once before the cycle opens, then leave the form alone until the cycle closes.


1. **Replace the competencies with yours.** If your organization already has a values or competency framework, use those exact words. Two competing vocabularies in one company is worse than a generic one.
2. **Cap the list at six.** More than six competencies and reviewers start rating from impression rather than evidence. Cut the ones that overlap.
3. **Define the evidence you expect.** Write one line under each competency saying what counts: a project, a metric, a specific occasion. This single step does more for rating quality than any other change.
4. **Decide what the rating drives.** If the overall rating feeds compensation, say so on the form. If it does not, say that too. Ambiguity here is where trust is lost.
5. **Adjust for level, not for person.** A senior engineer and a first-year engineer can share the form as long as “meets expectations” is defined against their own level. Never change the scale for an individual.
6. **Cut fields that no one reads.** If last cycle’s forms have an empty section in eighty percent of cases, delete it rather than reminding managers to fill it in.
7. **Check the form for role bias.** Prompts that reward visibility, meeting presence or hours favor some roles over others. Rewrite them to reward outcomes.
8. **Pilot with three managers.** Have them fill it in for one person each and time it. If the form takes over forty minutes, it will be rushed at scale.


For choosing the competencies themselves, the[performance review competencies](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/performance-review-competencies-examples/) guide has definitions you can lift directly into the form.

## Questions and examples to use with the template


The form sets the structure. The questions inside it decide whether you get anything useful. These six work in most manager reviews and can be dropped straight into the competency or summary sections.


- Which piece of work this period had the biggest impact, and what made it work?
- Where did results fall short of what we agreed, and what was in your control?
- What has this person got better at since the last review, with an example?
- What would have to change for this person to operate at the next level?
- What is the one thing you would ask them to do differently next quarter?
- What support have they asked for that they have not received?


For a full set sorted by review type and seniority, see the[performance review questions](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/performance-review-questions-2026/) library. When it comes to writing the answers, the difference is usually specificity: “consistently delivers high quality work” says nothing, while “shipped the billing migration two weeks early with zero rollback incidents” can be checked. The[performance review examples](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/performance-review-examples/) library has phrases at each rating level for nine competencies.


## Why standardize the review template


Three reasons to run one standard form rather than letting each manager write their own review forms, and none of them is that templates save time, although they do.


- **Comparability.** If every manager writes their own form, calibration is comparing prose to prose. A shared scale and shared competencies are what make a calibration meeting possible at all.
- **Completeness.** A form with a development section gets a development conversation. Free-text reviews reliably skip the parts the reviewer finds awkward.
- **Defensibility.** When a rating drives pay or a promotion decision, the evidence field beside it is the record. That record matters most in exactly the cases where it is least pleasant to write.


One correction worth making, because it is repeated everywhere: a template does not automate anything. It standardizes the form. Distribution, reminders, collecting responses, chasing the ones that are late and reporting on the result are software jobs. If you are running reviews for more than about forty people in a spreadsheet, that distinction starts to cost real time. For the wider picture of how reviews fit together, see the[employee performance reviews](https://www.peoplebox.ai/blog/effective-employee-performance-reviews-guide/) guide.

FAQs


### What should a performance review template include?


At minimum: employee and reviewer details, the review period, a defined rating scale, goals with targets and results, competencies with an evidence field beside every rating, strengths, areas to improve, development goals for the next period, a reviewer summary with an overall rating, employee comments and an acknowledgement. The evidence field is the one most forms leave out and the one that makes a rating defensible.


### Can I get a performance review template in Word or Google Docs?


Yes. The Word file at the top of this page is an editable .docx you can open in Word, Google Docs or Pages. There is also a printable PDF. If you would rather not download anything, the full template is written out in plain text further down the page and can be copied straight into your own document.


### What is the difference between a performance review template and an evaluation form?


In practice, nothing. Performance review template, performance evaluation form, performance appraisal form and employee review form are different names for the same artifact. Some organizations use appraisal for the annual pay-linked review and review for the wider conversation, but the underlying form is the same. Use whichever term your organization already uses.


### How do I customize a performance review template for different roles?


Change the competencies and the evidence you expect, not the scale. Replace the generic competencies with your own framework, cap the list at six, and write one line under each saying what counts as evidence in that role. Define meets expectations against the person’s own level so a first-year and a senior employee can share one form.


### What rating scale should a performance review form use?


A 5-point scale suits most organizations: not meeting, partially meeting, meeting, exceeding and outstanding. Use a 3-point scale for small teams or a first cycle, a 4-point scale when you want to remove the safe midpoint, and behaviorally anchored ratings when managers interpret a competency very differently. Whichever you choose, write the definitions into the form itself.


### How long should a performance review form take to complete?


Aim for twenty to forty minutes per employee for an annual review and around fifteen minutes for a quarterly check-in. If your pilot managers take longer than forty minutes, the form has too many fields and will be rushed at scale. Cut any section that came back empty for most employees in the last cycle.


### Do I need separate templates for self, peer and manager reviews?


You need the same structure with different prompts. The manager version carries the evidence and the final rating. The self-review asks what the employee attempted, learned and needs. The peer version asks only about observed working behavior and drops the overall rating entirely. All three variants are on this page.


### Is this performance review template free to use?


Yes. It is free to copy, edit and reuse inside your organization, including in commercial settings, and no email address is required to download it. The Peoplebox mark in the header and the credit line in the footer are ordinary editable elements, so delete them if you would rather circulate the form unbranded.
